title: Slide the tip of a triangle
hook: Drag a triangle's top corner far off to one side. Does it hold more, or less?

knows: area of a rectangle as width × height, counted in grid squares
doesNotKnow: that every triangle is half a base × height rectangle, however slanted

misconception: A lopsided triangle has a different area from an upright one on the same base and height.
objective: The learner can explain that sliding the top corner along a line parallel to the base keeps the base and height, so the area stays base × height ÷ 2 (here 12).

claims.text: A triangle with base 6 and height 4 has area 12 squares wherever its top corner sits on the line 4 above the base (tried from 6 left of the base to 6 past its end).
claims.source: Shoelace area of (0,0), (6,0), (x,4) is |6·4|/2 = 12 for every x. Demo.tsx shoelace(corners(x)); node gives 12 for x = −6, −3, 0, 3, 6, 9, 12.

claims.text: With the tip over the base, its drop line cuts the 6 × 4 box in two and the triangle is half of each part: half of 24.
claims.source: Each part is a rectangle split by its diagonal into two equal right triangles. 6 × 4 = 24, 24 / 2 = 12.

claims.text: Sliding the tip, each line across the triangle keeps its length and only shifts sideways, so the total area cannot change.
claims.source: At height y the cross-section has length 6(1 − y/4), independent of the tip's x (Demo.tsx strip lines at y = 1, 2, 3). Cavalieri's principle: equal cross-sections give equal areas.

claims.text: Any triangle's area is base × height ÷ 2.
claims.source: Standard result (Euclid, Elements I.41: a triangle is half a parallelogram on the same base and between the same parallels).

recall.question: Two triangles share a base of 10 cm and both reach 3 cm high. One is upright, one leans far over. Which has more area?
recall.why: Same base, same height: 10 × 3 ÷ 2 = 15 for both. Leaning only shifts each slice sideways.
